vengeful-spirit.name: Vengeful Spirit
vengeful-spirit.guideHtml:
Vengeful Spirit remains a solid support‑initiator with a 53.1% win rate across 492,403 ranked games on patch 7.41, making her a reliable pick in the current meta. Her toolkit—Magic Missile, Wave of Terror, Vengeance Aura, and Nether Swap—lets her dictate lane dynamics, set up kills, and protect carries. While she excels against heroes like Morphling and Slardar, she struggles versus heavy‑disruption picks such as Beastmaster and Clockwerk.

How to Play Vengeful Spirit

Laning Phase

  • Use Wave of Terror early to lower enemy armor and grant vision, making it easier to land Magic Missile stuns on squishy lane opponents.
  • Pair Magic Missile with a support’s disable (e.g., Lion’s Earth Spike) to guarantee burst kills on low‑HP heroes; the stun also secures last‑hits for your carry.
  • Position near your carry to apply Vengeance Aura, boosting their early damage output and making lane trades favorable.
  • When the enemy lane has a strong initiator (e.g., Beastmaster), keep Nether Swap ready to pull their off‑lane hero into your tower or swap them onto a dangerous enemy (like a roaming support).
  • Prioritize pulling the enemy creep wave with Nether Swap into your tower if you lack lane control, buying time for your safe‑lane carry to farm.

Mid Game

  • Hit level 6 and start roaming with Nether Swap to create pick‑offs; swapping an enemy into your team’s frontline or pulling a high‑value target into a tower often decides fights.
  • Use Wave of Terror in team fights to shred armor on enemy cores; combine with physical damage heroes (e.g., Faceless Void) for amplified burst.
  • Keep Vengeance Aura active on your core during sieges; the 20 % bonus damage on Vengeful herself makes her a surprising secondary damage source.
  • Time your Magic Missile stun on channeling heroes (e.g., Pugna, Enigma) to interrupt crucial ultimates and swing the fight.

Late Game

  • Focus on protecting your carry with Nether Swap—swap an enemy initiator onto your frontline or into a tower to neutralize their engage.
  • Position behind your frontline to maximize Vengeance Aura while staying safe from burst disables; remember the 20 % bonus damage on Vengeful herself can tip the scales in extended fights.
  • Avoid over‑extending without vision; a failed Nether Swap into a hidden enemy (e.g., Techies) can hand the enemy a cheap kill and swing the game.

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango — sustain in lane, especially against aggressive opponents.
  • Healing Salve — quick health recovery after early trades.
  • Observer Ward — provides vision for Wave of Terror and early map control.
  • Clarity — mana for spamming Magic Missile and Wave of Terror.

Core Items

  • Tranquil Boots — movement speed for roaming and a reliable health regen.
  • Magic Wand — burst of health/mana after frequent spell casts in team fights.
  • Glimmer Cape — defensive tool to save yourself or an ally after a Nether Swap into danger.
  • Force Staff — extra mobility for initiating swaps or escaping after a failed engage.

Situational Items

  • Aghanim’s Shard — upgrades Magic Missile with a longer stun and extra damage against heroes.
  • Lotus Orb — reflects single‑target spells, useful against Clockwerk and Techies.
  • Ghost Scepter — protects you from right‑click burst when you’re forced into melee range (e.g., against Dawnbreaker).
  • Eul’s Scepter — additional disable and self‑save; can combo with Nether Swap to lock down a target.
  • Aghanim’s Scepter — grants a second Nether Swap charge, dramatically increasing pick‑off potential in late‑game skirmishes.

Common Mistakes

  • Wasting Nether Swap on low‑impact targets – swapping a non‑threatening hero wastes a crucial cooldown that could have saved an ally or set up a kill.
  • Over‑committing without vision – using Nether Swap into fog of war often lands you in a trap set by Techies or Clockwerk.
  • Neglecting Vengeance Aura positioning – standing too far from your carry nullifies the aura’s damage boost, reducing lane pressure.
  • Spamming Magic Missile without mana management – running out of mana early forces you to rely on items alone, weakening your lane presence.

FAQ

Is Vengeful Spirit good in the current patch?

Yes. With a 53.1% win rate across nearly half a million ranked games, Vengeful Spirit is a strong support pick on patch 7.41, especially when paired with heroes that benefit from her Vengeance Aura and Nether Swap utility.

What lane does Vengeful Spirit play?

Vengeful Spirit is typically played in the safe lane as a support, using Wave of Terror and Vengeance Aura to empower the carry while providing early stun pressure with Magic Missile.

Who counters Vengeful Spirit?

Heroes with strong disables and burst—such as Beastmaster, Clockwerk, and Techies—currently give Vengeful Spirit the lowest win rates (≈36–38 %); they can punish her Nether Swap attempts and out‑scale her early game.
vengeful-spirit.counterHtml:
Vengeful Spirit thrives on her early‑game harassment and the damage boost she grants allies with Vengeance Aura and Wave of Terror. To shut her down you must neutralize her swap, survive her burst, and deny the aura’s uptime—typically by picking heroes that can lock her down, out‑range her, or force fights where her utility is irrelevant.

Why These Heroes Beat Vengeful Spirit

Beastmaster

Beastmaster’s Primal Roar and Wild Axes provide long‑range stuns and constant pressure, preventing Vengeful Spirit from safely swapping into allies. His Hawk Scout vision also negates the sight advantage from Wave of Terror. Tip: Use the Hawk to spot her swap attempts and time a Primal Roar right after a swap to punish the victim.

Clockwerk

Clockwerk’s Battery Assault and Hookshot lock Vengeful Spirit in place, nullifying her Nether Swap and forcing her to stay in the danger zone of his Power Cogs. The constant damage from the cog field also erodes her health faster than she can sustain with her aura. Tip: Initiate with Hookshot onto her or an ally she’s about to swap with, then follow with Battery Assault for a guaranteed kill.

Techies

Techies’ Remote Mines and Stasis Trap create invisible zones that punish Vengeful Spirit’s aggressive positioning; a well‑placed mine detonated on a swap can instantly kill her or force a retreat. Her Blast Off! also provides a burst escape that outpaces Vengeful Spirit’s swap range. Tip: Plant mines along common swap paths and keep a Stasis Trap ready to catch her when she tries to interrupt a channel.

Ringmaster (Rubick)

Rubick’s Telekinesis can lift Vengeful Spirit out of her swap range, and Spell Steal lets him turn her own Magic Missile or Wave of Terror back onto her team. By stealing her Nether Swap, Rubick can force a self‑swap that deals damage to both parties. Tip: Prioritize stealing Nether Swap early; a successful steal on a swap can instantly turn the fight.

Dawnbreaker

Dawnbreaker’s Starbreaker provides a large‑area stun that hits Vengeful Spirit even when she attempts to swap away, while Celestial Hammer grants her a shield that blocks the burst from Magic Missile. Her Luminosity aura also reduces incoming magic damage, mitigating Vengeful Spirit’s primary source of damage. Tip: Time Starbreaker to hit her just after a swap—she’ll be stunned and vulnerable to follow‑up damage.

Drafting Against Vengeful Spirit

  • Prioritize heroes with long‑range hard disables (stuns, roots, silences).
  • Pick tanky or burst‑resistant heroes that can survive the initial Magic Missile and Wave of Terror.
  • Include vision‑heavy picks (e.g., Hawk Scout, Sentry Wards) to negate her Wave of Terror sight.
  • Consider heroes that can steal or block Nether Swap (Rubick, Bane, Silencer).

Laning Against Vengeful Spirit

  • Trade early with ranged harass that outranges her Magic Missile; she struggles to land swaps when low on health.
  • Punish her when she attempts to swap onto you by positioning behind a creep wave or a tower—her swap will damage you and the tower blocks the follow‑up.
  • Keep a ward on the river to spot her Wave of Terror vision and avoid walking into her aura’s damage zone.
  • Force her to use Nether Swap defensively; once on cooldown, you can engage without fear of a surprise reposition.

Itemizing Against Vengeful Spirit

Force Staff — lets you escape a dangerous swap or reposition to avoid Magic Missile.
Eul's Scepter of Divinity — cyclones Vengeful Spirit, nullifying her swap and giving you time to kill her.
Ghost Scepter — makes you ethereal, preventing the damage from her Magic Missile and the swap‑damage burst.
Glimmer Cape — provides magic resistance and invisibility, allowing you to dodge Wave of Terror and survive her burst.

venomancer.name: Venomancer
venomancer.guideHtml:
Venomancer is a magic‑damage, area‑control support whose toolkit revolves around poison — damage over time, slows, and strong zoning. In the current 7.41 meta his overall win rate sits at 47.0% across 286 k recent ranked games, making him a solid but not dominant pick.

How to Play Venomancer

Laning Phase

  • Harass with Venomous Gale early; the line skillshot applies initial damage and a 3‑second DOT that forces melee opponents to trade poorly.
  • Stack Snakebite on the enemy off‑lane hero; each attack refreshes the toxin and deals extra damage when the target attacks, punishing aggressive heroes like Ember Spirit and Puck (who are currently his toughest matchups).
  • Use Poison Sting on creep waves to keep lane equilibrium low while still applying a slow that helps you and your carry avoid ganks.
  • Place early Plague Wards in the jungle brush; they are magic‑immune and can scout or deter rotations from heroes such as Invoker and Pudge.
  • Prioritize vision and warding because many of your toughest opponents (e.g., Batrider, Pudge) rely on surprise ganks.

Mid Game

  • Hit your power spike at level 6 – Noxious Plague now scales with max health, turning you into a massive team‑fight threat.
  • Group with your cores and drop Plague Wards in high‑traffic areas (Roshan, enemy jungle) to force fights and provide constant damage.
  • Use Venomous Gale + Noxious Plague combo on clustered enemies; the initial burst followed by health‑scaled DOT can swing team fights, especially against melee‑heavy lineups like Dragon Knight.
  • Push lanes with wards while your carry farms; the wards’ 50 % damage still chips towers and keeps the map pressured.

Late Game

  • Win condition: lock down team‑fight fronts with Noxious Plague and a wall of Plague Wards; the combined DOT can out‑damage many late‑game cores.
  • Position behind front‑liners; your low HP and lack of escape make you vulnerable to burst from Ember Spirit, Invoker, or Puck.
  • Avoid being the primary initiator; let tanks start the fight and then flood the battlefield with your poison.

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango — sustain for the long laning phase.
  • Healing Salve — quick health recovery after early harass.
  • Observer Ward — essential vision against gank‑heavy heroes.
  • Iron Branch ×2 — cheap stats and can later be built into Magic Wand.

Core Items

  • Aghanim’s Scepter — upgrades Noxious Plague to spread to nearby enemies, dramatically increasing team‑fight impact.
  • Glimmer Cape — provides needed magic immunity to survive burst from Ember Spirit, Invoker, and Puck.
  • Force Staff — helps you reposition wards and escape dangerous gaps from Batrider or Pudge.
  • Eul’s Scepter — offers a self‑save and a way to set up Noxious Plague on high‑HP targets.

Situational Items

  • Guardian Greaves — if your team lacks sustain and you need to counter heavy physical damage (e.g., Pudge).
  • Lotus Orb — reflects targeted spells like Batrider’s Flaming Lasso or Pug’s Meat Hook.
  • Aether Lens — extends the range of Venomous Gale and Noxious Plague, useful against long‑range heroes like Zeus.
  • Scythe of Vyse — additional hard‑disable when you need extra control against mobile heroes like Ember Spirit.
  • Pipe of Insight — against teams with heavy magical burst (Invoker, Queen of Pain).

Common Mistakes

  • Over‑extending without wards – many low‑MMR players forget to place Plague Wards, leaving them vulnerable to ganks from Batrider and Pudge.
  • Using Snakebite as a kill‑steal – the ability’s damage is modest; it’s better saved for applying toxin on high‑HP targets before a team fight.
  • Stacking too many wards early – neglects personal survivability; a balanced mix of wards and defensive items (Glimmer, Force Staff) is crucial.
  • Failing to time Noxious Plague – casting it too early wastes its health‑scaled damage; wait until the enemy team is grouped.

FAQ

Is Venomancer good in the current patch?

Yes. With a 47 % win rate on 286 k recent ranked matches, Venomancer is a solid support choice. His poison‑based damage scales well into the late game, and his win rates are especially high against heroes like Clockwerk (63.9 %) and Warlock (63.5 %).

What lane does Venomancer play?

Venomancer is typically played in the safelane support position (position 5), but he can also function as a roaming support (position 4) when the safelane carries are strong early. His lane presence is defined by constant harassment with Venomous Gale and Snakebite.

Who counters Venomancer?

Heroes with high burst or strong gap‑close tend to dominate him: Ember Spirit (37.5 % win), Batrider (41.3 %), Invoker (41.7 %), Pudge (41.8 %), Queen of Pain (42.7 %), and Puck (43.5 %) are currently his toughest matchups. Building defensive items and maintaining vision are essential to survive their pressure.
venomancer.counterHtml:
Venomancer’s strength lies in his relentless poison damage and the zone‑control his Plague Wards provide, forcing enemies to constantly heal or suffer massive health loss over time. The key to shutting him down is to apply burst damage, purge his toxins quickly, and pressure him before he can stack wards and spread Noxious Plague.

Why These Heroes Beat Venomancer

Ember Spirit

Ember’s Sleight of Hand and Flame Guard let him dodge Venomous Gale and instantly purge poison with the shield’s magic resistance, while his burst from Fire Remnant and Seismic Wave outdamage the slow‑based harassment. Tip: Use a Fire Remnant to jump over the line of Gale, then unleash Seismic Wave to force Venomancer’s wards to die quickly.

Batrider

Batrider’s Flamebreak provides a strong magic‑damage purge and a knock‑back that can pull Venomancer out of his ward‑protected zone, while Sticky Napalm amplifies physical damage against the already‑slowed target. Tip: Land Flamebreak on Venomancer right after he casts Gale to remove the poison and set up a quick kill.

Invoker

Invoker’s Cold Snap and EMP burst the health pool that Noxious Plague scales off, and Sun Strike bypasses any movement‑speed slow to finish him from afar. Tip: Cast Cold Snap on Venomancer right after he lands a Gale; the rapid stuns prevent him from re‑applying poison while EMP drains his health.

Pudge

Pudge’s Meat Hook can yank Venomancer out of his ward‑dense area, and Rot deals massive magic damage that stacks on the poison tick, quickly overwhelming his health regeneration. Tip: Hook Venomancer when he’s casting Gale—he’ll be immobilized and take the full Rot damage while his wards die.

Queen of Pain

QoP’s Scream of Pain and Sonic Wave deliver pure magical burst that ignores Venomancer’s magic‑immune wards, and her Blink lets her dodge Gale’s line and close the distance for a quick kill. Tip: Blink behind Venomancer after his Gale, then unleash Sonic Wave to purge and burst him before he can place another ward.

Drafting Against Venomancer

  • Prioritize heroes with strong magic purge or instant burst (e.g., Ember Spirit, Batrider, Queen of Pain).
  • Include at least one hero with high mobility to dodge Venomous Gale lines.
  • Consider picking a tank with high magic resistance to mitigate poison damage early.
  • Avoid stacking multiple melee heroes that rely on sustained fights, as Venomancer thrives in prolonged engagements.

Laning Against Venomancer

  • Harass him before he can stack a ward; his early game damage is limited.
  • Use spells that provide magic immunity or purge (e.g., Flamebreak, Cold Snap) to neutralize his poison on the spot.
  • Trade when he casts Snakebite—attack immediately after the damage tick to capitalize on his brief cooldown.
  • Force him to use his limited mana on Gale/Poison Sting, then punish the cooldown window with a burst combo.

Itemizing Against Venomancer

Manta Style — creates a duplicate that can purge poison and forces Venomancer to split his ward focus.
Black King Bar — grants magic immunity, nullifying all poison damage and allowing you to ignore his slows.
Eul’s Scepter of Divinity — cyclone removes Venomancer’s toxins and disrupts his casting rhythm.
Diffusal Blade — burns mana, limiting his ability to spam Gale and Noxious Plague.

viper.name: Viper
viper.guideHtml:
Viper is a durable, lane‑dominating hero who excels at applying lethal poison pressure and surviving burst damage. In the current 7.41 meta his overall pub win rate sits at 48.3% over 295,933 ranked games, placing him as a solid but not dominant pick in the carry/disabler slot.

How to Play Viper

Laning Phase

  • Poison Attack stacks up to 6 × slow and magic‑resist reduction; harass early and force enemy creep aggro to secure lane control.
  • Use Nethertoxin on the creep wave to deny enemy last‑hits and punish heroes that rely on attack speed (e.g., Slardar, Bane).
  • Corrosive Skin gives you a passive health‑drain on attackers; play aggressively against melee heroes that will trade hits, but keep a safe distance from Techies mines.
  • Prioritize a mid‑lane or safe‑lane position against hard‑counters like Zeus and Windranger; their burst can outpace your early damage.
  • When the enemy supports roam, drop a quick Nosedive to apply a burst of Nethertoxin and trigger Corrosive Skin on multiple foes.

Mid Game

  • Power spike at level 6 with Viper Strike—use it to lock down high‑damage cores (e.g., Primal Beast) and force them to retreat.
  • Group with your team to place Nethertoxin in chokepoints; the damage over time scales with duration, making it deadly in prolonged fights.
  • After acquiring Aghanim’s Shard, upgrade Nosedive to add a 4‑second Corrosive Skin splash, turning it into a strong team‑fight initiation tool.
  • Push split‑push lanes with Poison Attack stacks; the movement‑slow makes it hard for enemy cores to contest without risking a Viper Strike lock.

Late Game

  • Win condition: lock down the enemy carry with Viper Strike while your team follows up with burst; the combined poison and magic‑resist reduction lets you survive otherwise lethal spells.
  • Position near the front of fights to let Corrosive Skin punish any hero that dives you; stay just out of range of Techies' mines and Zeus' lightning.
  • Losing the game often stems from over‑extending without vision—enemy teams can flank and burst you before your poison ticks out.

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango + Healing Salve — sustain for early lane harassment.
  • Slippers of Agility — early damage for stacking Poison Attack.
  • Iron Branch x2 — cheap stats and can be later built into a Magic Wand.

Core Items

  • Power Treads — flexible stats; switch to strength for survivability against burst.
  • Dragon Lance — provides range and agility, boosting poison damage and allowing safer Viper Strike casts.
  • Manta Style — dispels silences (e.g., from Silencer) and adds extra attack speed for faster stack buildup.
  • Black King Bar — essential against magic‑heavy lineups (Zeus, Ancient Apparition) that can otherwise burst you.

Situational Items

  • Aghanim’s Shard — upgrades Nosedive with a Corrosive Skin splash, great for team fights.
  • Linken’s Sphere — blocks single‑target disables from Bane or Zeus.
  • Satanic — massive survivability when you’re the primary focus in late‑game fights.
  • Scythe of Vyse — adds extra hard‑disable when you need to lock down slippery heroes like Windranger.
  • Lotus Orb — reflects targeted spells and provides armor against physical burst (Slardar).
  • Gleipnir — combines root and slow, synergizing with your existing poison slows.

Common Mistakes

  • Over‑relying on basic attacks without stacking Poison Attack; the damage ramp is the core of Viper’s lane dominance.
  • Using Viper Strike too early on heroes with high burst (Techies, Zeus) and then getting killed before the poison ticks.
  • Neglecting vision around objectives; enemy teams can ambush you while you’re focused on stacking poison.
  • Building too much damage early and forgetting defensive items like BKB or Satanic, leading to easy deaths against magic burst.

FAQ

Is Viper good in the current patch?

Yes. Viper sits at a 48.3% win rate on the latest ranked data, making him a viable pick, especially against heroes he can out‑poison such as Bristleback and Silencer.

What lane does Viper play?

Viper is most effective in the safe lane (radiant or dire) or as a mid‑lane hero, where he can safely stack Poison Attack and control the wave with Nethertoxin.

Who counters Viper?

The toughest matchups right now are Techies (36.5% win), Bane (38.2%), Slardar (39.7%), Zeus (40.4%), and Windranger (42.5%)—all heroes that can either burst him before his poison ticks or out‑maneuver his slows.
viper.counterHtml:
Viper’s threat comes from his relentless poison‑based damage and the way his abilities stack slows, magic‑resistance reduction, and damage‑over‑time. The core way to shut him down is to deny him the sustained fights he thrives on and to exploit the moments when his passive Corrosive Skin is on cooldown.

Why These Heroes Beat Viper

Techies

Techies’ Stasis Trap and Remote Mines force Viper to move constantly, breaking the stacking mechanic of Poison Attack and preventing him from maintaining a safe distance. Tip: place mines near Viper’s typical farming spots and use Stasis Trap to lock him down before he can activate Nosedive.

Bane

Bane’s Nightmare and Fiend’s Grip silence Viper, cancelling the channel of Nosedive and stopping the application of new poison stacks. Tip: initiate with Nightmare as soon as Viper steps into lane, then follow with Fiend’s Grip to force a long‑duration silence.

Slardar

Slardar’s Slithereen Crush provides a hard‑stop stun that interrupts Viper’s Nosedive and removes his movement‑speed slow, while Amplify Damage reduces Viper’s armor, making his physical attacks far more lethal. Tip: time the crush right after Viper casts Nethertoxin to catch him while his poison is still ticking.

Zeus

Zeus’s Arc Lightning and Lightning Bolt deal pure magic damage that ignores Viper’s magic‑resistance boost from Corrosive Skin, and his constant burst forces Viper to retreat before he can stack enough poison. Tip: use Lightning Bolt on Viper when he is mid‑Nosedive to interrupt the channel and punish the long cooldown.

Primal Beast

Primal Beast’s Trample and Onslaught grant massive burst and a displacement that breaks Viper’s positioning, while his Uproar reduces enemy armor, making Viper’s physical damage from items like Desolator deadly. Tip: engage with Trample as soon as Viper steps into range; the knock‑up interrupts Nosedive and forces a reset of his poison stacks.

Drafting Against Viper

  • Prioritize heroes with reliable silences or stuns (e.g., Bane, Lion, Silencer).
  • Pick high‑burst magic damage heroes that can outrange his poison (e.g., Zeus, Lina).
  • Include mobile heroes that can dodge Nosedive and Nethertoxin (e.g., Slark, Ember Spirit).
  • Consider bans that remove his primary lane partner, especially heroes that synergize with his poison (e.g., Bristleback).

Laning Against Viper

  • Harass early before Poison Attack reaches 6 stacks; his damage spikes dramatically after that.
  • Trade when Viper’s Corrosive Skin is on cooldown (after he’s been hit or after using Nosedive).
  • Force him to use Nosedive defensively by zoning him with creep aggro or early tower pressure.
  • Pull the lane to deny him safe farm and to make his poison stacks fall off due to distance.

Itemizing Against Viper

Black King Bar — blocks the magic damage from Nethertoxin and Viper Strike, letting you trade freely.
Manta Style — dispels Corrosive Skin’s slow and magic‑resistance reduction while providing split‑push pressure.
Eul’s Scepter — silences Viper for 2.5 seconds, cancelling Nosedive and allowing you to dodge poison ticks.
Aghanim’s Shard (for heroes like Lion) — adds an extra stun or silence that further interrupts Viper’s channeling.

visage.name: Visage
visage.guideHtml:
Visage is a high‑utility support whose game hinges on controlling space with his Familiars and scaling damage through Soul Assumption. On patch 7.41 his 52 % win‑rate in ranked (54 k games) makes him a solid pick, especially on teams that can protect his early‑game fragility and capitalize on his mid‑game power spikes.

How to Play Visage

Laning Phase

  • Summon Familiars at level 1; keep them within 900 units of you to benefit from Gravekeeper’s Cloak and to start stacking Soul Assumption on enemy hero hits > 100 damage.
  • Use Grave Chill on the enemy off‑lane hero to sap their attack/move speed while feeding the debuff to your Familiars for a small speed boost—great against fast‑pushing cores like Axe (one of Visage’s tougher matchups, 40.9 % win).
  • Position Familiars behind your creep wave; they are blind but can still land Stone Form on clustered enemies when you spot a stun‑ready opportunity.
  • Prioritize landing Stone Form on enemy supports (e.g., Lion, Shadow Shaman) to secure early kills; the stun and damage also help you win lane trades.
  • Keep an eye on Soul Assumption charges; each time the enemy hero takes > 100 damage (from your attacks, Familiars, or tower hits) a charge is added—aim to hit them with a combo of auto‑attacks and Stone Form to maximize charge gain.

Mid Game

  • Power spike at level 12 (when you have 2 Familiars, Grave Chill, Soul Assumption, and Stone Form). Start roaming with your Familiars to secure objectives; their stun is excellent for gank setups.
  • Group with your team around Roshan; Stone Form from a Familiar can lock down the Roshan or enemy heroes, while Soul Assumption damage spikes dramatically after 4–5 charges.
  • When you have Aghanim’s Shard, upgrade Stone Form to reduce cooldown, allowing rapid stun‑damage cycles in team fights.
  • Avoid extended 1‑v‑1 duels against high‑burst heroes like Invoker (30 % win) or Templar Assassin (39.3 % win); instead, play around vision and use Grave Chill to blunt their damage output.

Late Game

  • Win condition: Use Familiars as mobile stun‑damage sources to lock down key enemy carries (e.g., Ursa, Timbersaw) while your team dishes out damage. Keep Familiars within 900 units of you so Gravekeeper’s Cloak continues to protect them.
  • Positioning: Stay behind your frontline; your Gravekeeper’s Cloak provides a damage barrier that can absorb burst from heroes like Axe or Shadow Fiend (43.5 % win).
  • Losing the game: Allow Familiars to be isolated or killed—once they die you lose your primary source of stun and damage, and you become an easy target for the enemy’s burst heroes.

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango — sustain in lane; Visage has low HP pool.
  • Healing Salve — quick recovery after early harass.
  • Observer Ward — vision to protect Familiars and set up Stone Form stuns.
  • Sentry Ward — counter enemy detection of Familiars.
  • Clarity — mana for early Grave Chill and Stone Form casts.

Core Items

  • Tranquil Boots — movement speed and passive HP regen; lets you chase or reposition Familiars safely.
  • Aghanim’s Shard — reduces Stone Form cooldown, increasing stun frequency.
  • Glimmer Cape — protects you and Familiars from burst (crucial vs Invoker, Axe).
  • Force Staff — creates distance for safe Stone Form placement and to pull yourself out of danger.

Situational Items

  • Aghanim’s Scepter — upgrades Soul Assumption to a stronger AoE burst; pick when you have many charges and need extra team‑fight damage.
  • Lotus Orb — reflects targeted spells (useful against Ogre Magi’s Bloodlust and Invoker’s Sun Strike).
  • Ghost Scepter — safety against right‑click heroes like Ursa and Timbersaw when you’re forced into melee.
  • Eul’s Scepter — additional disable and self‑save; works well with Stone Form to chain stuns.
  • Black King Bar — only on heavily magical lineups where you must stay in fights (e.g., against heavy spell damage from Invoker).

Common Mistakes

  • Leaving Familiars out of 900 range – they lose Gravekeeper’s Cloak protection and die quickly.
  • Using Stone Form on single targets – waste its AoE stun; always aim for clustered enemies or creep waves.
  • Over‑committing to lane fights against burst heroes (Ogre Magi, Invoker); Visage’s low HP makes early deaths common.
  • Neglecting Soul Assumption charge management – failing to stack charges reduces your mid‑game damage output dramatically.

FAQ

Is Visage good in the current patch?

Yes. With a 52 % win‑rate across 54 k ranked games, Visage is a reliable support. His strength lies in mid‑game team fights where Stone Form stuns and Soul Assumption damage can swing engagements.

What lane does Visage play?

Visage is typically played as a hard support in the safe lane (position 5) alongside a carry. This placement lets him farm Familiars safely, stack Soul Assumption, and provide early vision and disables.

Who counters Visage?

Heroes with high burst or strong disables—Ogre Magi, Invoker, Hoodwink, Templar Assassin, Axe, and Shadow Fiend—show the lowest win rates against him (25 %–44 %). Keeping distance, using Gravekeeper’s Cloak, and building defensive items are essential against these matchups.

Why These Heroes Beat Visage

Ogre Magi

Ogre’s Fireblast and Ignite provide instant stun and damage, killing Familiars before they can Stone Form, while his Bloodlust amplifies allied attack speed, overwhelming Visage’s low early‑game damage. Tip: land a Fireblast on the Familiar as soon as it appears and follow up with a Bloodlust‑boosted auto‑attack to force Visage to retreat.

Invoker

Invoker’s Cold Snap repeatedly stuns Familiars, preventing Stone Form and draining Visile’s Soul Assumption charges, while Sun Strike can punish Visage’s static positioning behind his cloak. Tip: use Cold Snap on the Familiar and quickly switch to a damaging combo (e.g., Sun Strike + EMP) to force Visage to waste his cloak on hero damage.

Hoodwink

Acorn Shot and Bushwhack apply strong slows and a hard root, making it impossible for Familiars to close distance for Stone Form; Scurry grants Hoodwink the mobility to dodge Visage’s Grave Chill and stay out of his 900‑range cloak protection. Tip: trap the Familiar with Bushwhack, then follow with Acorn Shot to burst it before it can stun.

Templar Assassin

Templar’s Refraction blocks the initial damage from Familiars and Psi Blades shred Visage’s health from range, while Meld lets her jump behind his cloak, denying him the safety zone for his Familiars. Tip: wait for Visage to cast Stone Form, then Meld behind him and burst with Refraction‑enhanced attacks.

Axe

Axe’s Berserker’s Call forces Visage and his Familiars to attack a tanky target, instantly breaking the Familiar’s Stone Form channel and triggering Culling Blade for a quick kill. His Counter Helix punishes any melee attempts to close the gap. Tip: initiate with Call as soon as the Familiar appears, then follow up with a Culling Blade to eliminate Visage’s frontline.

Drafting Against Visage

  • Prioritize heroes with hard disables that can stun or root Familiars (e.g., stun‑heavy supports, burst mages).
  • Pick heroes with strong early‑game damage or true‑damage spikes to force Visage to burn his cloak.
  • Include at least one mobile hero that can outrange the 900‑unit cloak radius.
  • Consider banning heroes that synergize with Visage’s Familiars (e.g., high‑damage melee carries).

Laning Against Visage

  • Harass Familiars aggressively; a single stun or root kills them before Stone Form.
  • Trade when Visage is out of his 900‑range cloak—he loses the protective layer and becomes vulnerable.
  • Force him to use Grave Chill on creeps or towers, denying the speed boost to his Familiars.
  • Push the lane early to deny space for Familiars to spawn and gain charges for Soul Assumption.

Itemizing Against Visage

Force Staff — pulls Visage out of his cloak radius, breaking his defensive layer and exposing him to damage.
Eul’s Scepter of Divinity – cyclones Familiars and Visage, preventing Stone Form and resetting Soul Assumption charge buildup.
Ghost Scepter – makes you untargetable by Familiars’ physical attacks and Stone Form damage.
Heaven’s Halberd – disarms Visage, stopping his ability to cast Grave Chill or Stone Form while you focus his Familiars.

void-spirit.name: Void Spirit
void-spirit.guideHtml:
Void Spirit is a highly mobile, burst‑damage hero who excels at diving in, disrupting, and escaping. In patch 7.41 his overall pub win rate sits at 49.2% over 158,955 ranked games, placing him as a solid but not dominant pick in the current meta.

How to Play Void Spirit

Laning Phase

  • Use Astral Step to harass and secure last hits; the void mark slows enemies, making them vulnerable to follow‑up damage.
  • Drop Aether Remnant near enemy creep equilibrium to punish opponents who overextend, especially against melee supports that lack blink.
  • Dissimilate can be cast defensively to dodge early ganks; the portal exit damage also deters aggressive lane opponents.
  • Pair Resonant Pulse with a short burst of auto‑attacks to trade with heroes that rely on physical damage (e.g., Sven, Earthshaker).
  • Prioritize a balanced attribute spread early so Intrinsic Edge scales your damage and survivability from the start.

Mid Game

  • Hit level 6 and acquire Astral Step talent for longer range; this opens up 2‑v‑2 skirmishes and split‑push potential.
  • Look for Dissimilate + Aether Remnant combos on isolated targets; the pull and portal damage often secure kills before the enemy can react.
  • Roam after securing a lane advantage; your mobility lets you gank hard‑carries like Zeus or Weaver, where you have a >60% win rate.
  • Control vision around Roshan with Aether Remnant to set up safe grabs on enemy supports attempting to contest.

Late Game

  • Focus on pick‑off plays: use Astral Step to jump onto the backline, apply Aether Remnant to lock down a carry, and follow with Dissimilate for burst.
  • Position near the front of team fights to let Resonant Pulse soak physical hits while your damage pulses out, but avoid staying too long against high‑damage nukes (e.g., Phoenix).
  • Lose the game if you overcommit without a clear escape path; the enemy’s crowd‑control (Nyx Assassin, Necrophos) can quickly turn a dive into a death.

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango — sustain in lane, especially against harass from ranged supports.
  • Healing Salve — quick health recovery after early skirmishes.
  • Iron Branch ×2 — cheap attribute boost for Intrinsic Edge scaling.
  • Faerie Fire — emergency burst damage and a small health buffer.

Core Items

  • Phase Boots — adds attack speed, damage, and the extra mobility needed for aggressive Astral Step combos.
  • Eul’s Scepter of Divinity — provides mana, movement speed, and a reliable self‑disable to set up Aether Remnant pulls.
  • Black King Bar — essential against heavy magical burst (Phoenix, Necrophos) and disables that can nullify your mobility.
  • Aghanim’s Scepter — upgrades Dissimilate to create additional portals, increasing damage output and escape options.

Situational Items

  • Satanic — massive survivability when you’re forced into the front line against tanky heroes like Alchemist.
  • Linken’s Sphere — blocks single‑target disables from Nyx Assassin or Phoenix.
  • Scythe of Vyse — adds hard crowd‑control to lock down slippery carries such as Lycan.
  • Manta Style — counters silences and provides extra Astral Step dash distance.
  • Heart of Tarrasque — boosts HP for prolonged fights when you’re the primary damage dealer.

Common Mistakes

  • Over‑extending without a remnant – diving without placing Aether Remnant lets enemies escape or counter‑initiate.
  • Wasting Dissimilate on creeps – the portal damage is far more effective on heroes; use it to finish low‑HP opponents.
  • Neglecting BKB – against magic‑heavy lineups (Phoenix, Necrophos) you’ll die instantly after a single burst.
  • Poor positioning of Astral Step – jumping too far into the enemy front line without an exit path often results in being caught by crowd‑control.

FAQ

Is Void Spirit good in the current patch?

Yes. His 49.2% win rate across nearly 160 k ranked games shows he’s a viable pick, especially against heroes like Zeus (64.9% win) and Sven (62.9% win). However, he struggles versus heavy disables such as Nyx Assassin and Necrophos.

What lane does Void Spirit play?

Void Spirit is most commonly played in the mid lane as a solo carry, but he can also be effective in the off‑lane when paired with a strong support who can provide vision for his Aether Remnant setups.

Who counters Void Spirit?

The toughest matchups are Nyx Assassin, Necrophos, Phoenix, Treant Protector, Alchemist, and Lycan, where Void Spirit’s win rates drop into the low‑30s percent range. These heroes either lock him down with disables or out‑scale his burst damage.
void-spirit.counterHtml:
Void Spirit’s strength lies in his extreme mobility and burst‑damage combo: Astral Step, Dissimilate and Aether Remnant let him zip in, lock down a target and explode for massive damage. To shut him down you must deny those tools—lock him down, survive his burst, and punish his low early‑game health pool.

Why These Heroes Beat Void Spirit

Nyx Assassin

Nyx’s Mana Burn instantly drains Void Spirit’s limited mana, preventing multiple uses of Astral Step and Dissimilate, while Spiked Carapace reflects the physical damage from Void’s burst. Tip: land a Vendetta from fog of war right after Void’s Aether Remnant lands to catch him while his shield is on cooldown.

Necrophos

Necrophos’s Heartstopper Aura continuously saps Void’s health, making his early‑game skirmishes lethal, and Reaper’s Scythe provides a long‑duration stun that outlasts Void’s shield from Resonant Pulse. Tip: force a 2‑v‑1 fight and let Necro’s damage over time wear Void down before committing to a kill.

Phoenix

Phoenix’s Supernova creates a large, un‑targetable zone that blocks Void’s Astral Step pathing and forces him to waste Aether Remnant on a harmless unit. Additionally, Sun Ray provides constant magical damage that bypasses Void’s physical shield. Tip: wait for Void to commit his burst, then activate Supernova to trap him and force a long‑duration fight.

Treant Protector

Treant’s Nature’s Guise grants invisibility and Living Armor gives high physical damage mitigation, nullifying Void’s burst and allowing safe counter‑engagements. His Overgrowth stun also disables Void’s mobility, making him an easy target. Tip: use Overgrowth right after Void lands Astral Step to lock him down before he can escape.

Alchemist

Alchemist’s Chemical Rage gives massive health regeneration and damage reduction, letting him survive Void’s initial combo, while Acid Spray applies a lingering damage‑over‑time that punishes Void’s low sustain. Tip: build Aghanim’s Shard for the extra burst and force Void to waste his cooldowns on a tanky Alchemist.

Drafting Against Void Spirit

  • Prioritize heroes with strong disables (stuns, silences) that can interrupt Astral Step or Dissimilate.
  • Pick high‑HP or magic‑immune heroes to survive his burst (e.g., Treant, Alchemist, Necrophos).
  • Include mana‑burn or mana‑drain abilities to limit his ability spam.
  • Avoid picking multiple early‑game squishies that Void can quickly eliminate.

Laning Against Void Spirit

  • Harass him when his Resonant Pulse shield is on cooldown; his early HP pool is very low.
  • Trade with ranged poke that forces him to use Astral Step defensively, wasting his mobility.
  • Punish his Aether Remnant placement by staying out of its line of sight or baiting it onto creeps.
  • Force early 2‑v‑1 fights where your sustain or burst can outpace his combo.

Itemizing Against Void Spirit

Ghost Scepter — blocks Void’s physical burst from Astral Step and Dissimilate, forcing him to rely on magic damage he rarely has.
Eul’s Scepter of Divinity – cyclone interrupts his combo and removes the Aether Remnant threat while buying time for a counter‑engage.
Pipe of Insight – magic resistance mitigates the damage from his Aether Remnant pull and any magical follow‑up from allies.
Lotus Orb – reflects targeted disables back onto Void, preventing him from locking you down with stuns or silences.

warlock.name: Warlock
warlock.guideHtml:
Warlock remains a reliable support‑initiator in the current meta, sitting at a 49.2% win rate across 251 k recent ranked games. His toolkit—Fatal Bonds, Shadow Word, Upheaval, and a durable Golem—makes him a strong team‑fight presence, though he still struggles against mobile, bursty heroes.

How to Play Warlock

Laning Phase

  • Use Fatal Bonds on the enemy off‑lane and any nearby creeps to spread damage and force the opponent to trade poorly.
  • Drop Shadow Word on yourself or your carry for sustain; the heal scales with your level, making lane survivability easy against hard‑lane matchups.
  • When the lane is contested, channel Upheaval to zone the enemy and deny farm; the slow persists for 1 s after the channel ends, helping you and your carry disengage.
  • Prioritize pulling the small camp early and use Eldritch Summoning to spawn imps on enemy deaths, adding extra damage and lane pressure.
  • Against tough matchups like Keeper of the Light or Slark (Warlock win ≈ 30‑35% in those lanes), play ultra‑defensive: keep Shadow Word on yourself, avoid aggressive Fatal Bonds, and request early support from your off‑lane.

Mid Game

  • Power spike at level 6 with Chaotic Offering; look for 2‑v‑2 skirmishes where the Golem’s stun and permanent immolation can swing fights.
  • Secure vision around Roshan and high‑ground jungle; Warlock’s Upheaval combined with the Golem’s slow makes him excellent at contesting objectives.
  • Use Fatal Bonds on clustered enemy heroes before initiating with the Golem to maximize shared damage.
  • In lanes where you have an easy matchup (e.g., against Sand King, Drow Ranger), push towers aggressively after a successful Golem kill.

Late Game

  • Win condition: lock down the enemy backline with Chaotic Offering, then let the Golem and imps shred through team fights while your allies focus high‑value targets.
  • Positioning: stay just behind your front line; the Golem’s stun is short (0.8 s) but its damage over time is crucial, so you need to be close enough to cast Upheaval without being focused.
  • Losing the game often comes from over‑extending without vision; mobile heroes like Pudge or Venomancer can sidestep your Golem and burst you before you can land Fatal Bonds.

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango — basic sustain for the early lane.
  • Healing Salve — quick burst heal to survive early harass.
  • Observer Ward — vision to protect against ganks, especially versus mobile heroes.
  • Clarity — mana for frequent Shadow Word and Upheaval casts.

Core Items

  • Arcane Boots — reliable mana pool for constant spell usage.
  • Aghanim’s Scepter — upgrades Chaotic Offering to a larger Golem with longer stun and adds a second Golem after death, dramatically increasing team‑fight presence.
  • Guardian Greaves — provides armor, HP regen, and a strong team‑wide heal; synergizes with Shadow Word for sustain.

Situational Items

  • Glimmer Cape — against burst heroes like Slark or Pudge; grants temporary invisibility to survive focus fire.
  • Lotus Orb — reflects single‑target spells such as Keeper of the Light’s Will‑of‑the‑Wisp or Dazzle’s Shallow Grave.
  • Pipe of Insight — strong against magic‑heavy lineups (e.g., Venomancer, Ancient Apparition).
  • Force Staff — helps you escape or reposition to land Fatal Bonds on fleeing enemies.
  • Mekansm — alternative to Guardian Greaves when you need a cheaper team heal and armor.

Common Mistakes

  • Spamming Fatal Bonds without follow‑up – bonding enemies is useless if you can’t channel damage or secure a kill.
  • Over‑committing the Golem – diving into fights without vision lets mobile heroes dodge the stun and kill Warlock first.
  • Neglecting mana management – forgetting Arcane Boots or Clarity leads to being spell‑starved during crucial team fights.
  • Ignoring enemy mobility – playing aggressively against heroes like Slark, Pudge, or Keeper of the Light without proper defensive items (Glimmer Cape, Lotus Orb) often results in early deaths.

FAQ

Is Warlock good in the current patch?

Warlock sits at a 49.2% win rate on patch 7.41, making him a solid, though not dominant, support. His strength lies in team‑fight control and sustained damage, but he can be punished by highly mobile or bursty heroes.

What lane does Warlock play?

Warlock is typically played as a hard support in the safe lane, pairing with a carry to provide sustain and zoning. He can also be flexed to the off‑lane when a team needs additional initiation.

Who counters Warlock?

The toughest matchups are against mobile, burst heroes: Keeper of the Light (30.9% win), Slark (34.6%), Treant Protector (35.7%), Venomancer (36.5%), and Pudge (38.1%). Vision, defensive items, and careful positioning are essential to survive their pressure.
warlock.counterHtml:
Warlock’s threat comes from his ability to turn every kill into a cascade of damage and summons—Fatal Bonds spreads damage, Shadow Word heals allies while hurting foes, and Chaotic Offering adds a durable, damaging golem. The key to shutting him down is to deny him the kills and prolonged fights that trigger his imp spawns, and to apply constant pressure that forces him to waste his channelled Upheaval.

Why These Heroes Beat Warlock

Keeper of the Light

Keeper’s Illuminate and Chakra Magic give him high burst and sustain, while his Will‑of‑the‑Wisp provides a reliable escape from Warlock’s Upheaval channel. The constant damage and mobility prevent Warlock from landing Fatal Bonds on multiple heroes, and the extra mana regen lets Keeper spam spells to out‑damage Warlock’s Shadow Word heal. Tip: Use Chakra Magic to keep your mana high and force Warlock to waste his channel on a moving target.

Slark

Slark’s Dark Pact instantly removes the damage‑over‑time from Fatal Bonds and Shadow Word, and his Pounce lets him jump out of Upheaval’s radius. With Essence Shift, Slark can out‑heal Warlock’s heal‑on‑damage and turn Warlock’s own damage against him. Tip: Initiate with Pounce right after Warlock casts Upheaval; the brief stun forces him to channel longer while you slip out and purge his bonds.

Treant Protector

Treant’s Nature’s Grasp and Living Armor provide strong lane control and damage mitigation, making it hard for Warlock to land effective Fatal Bonds. The Overgrowth stun interrupts Warlock’s channelled Upheaval and prevents him from summoning imps on kills. Tip: Time Overgrowth just as Warlock begins Upheaval to lock him down and deny any kills that would spawn imps.

Venomancer

Venomancer’s Poison Nova and Venomous Gale apply continuous damage that outpaces Warlock’s heal‑on‑damage, while his Plague Ward provides vision and extra damage sources that force Warlock to split his Fatal Bonds. The slow from Poison Nova hampers Warlock’s ability to reposition for Upheaval. Tip: Place Plague Wards near Warlock’s pull‑line to punish his attempts to channel Upheaval safely.

Pudge

Pudge’s Meat Hook can pull Warlock out of his own Upheaval radius, instantly breaking Fatal Bonds on the pulled target. Rot applies constant damage that ignores Warlock’s heal‑on‑damage, and the Dismember stun forces Warlock to drop his channel. Tip: Hook Warlock right after he casts Fatal Bonds; the forced movement breaks the bond network and denies imp spawns.

Drafting Against Warlock

  • Prioritize heroes with strong single‑target burst or purge (e.g., Slark, Pudge, Silencer).
  • Pick mobile heroes that can dodge Upheaval’s channel (e.g., Keeper of the Light, Anti‑Mage).
  • Include heroes with reliable disables that can interrupt channelled spells (e.g., Lion, Shadow Demon).
  • Avoid picking multiple low‑damage, sustain‑heavy cores that let Warlock’s bonds thrive.

Laning Against Warlock

  • Harass early before Fatal Bonds can hit multiple units; Warlock’s damage is low pre‑level 2.
  • Force him to use Shadow Word on creeps instead of allies to waste its heal.
  • Trade when his Upheaval is on cooldown; his damage output drops sharply without the channel.
  • Punish his positioning: if he stands near his tower, use long‑range poke to force him to retreat and lose lane control.

Itemizing Against Warlock

Eul’s Scepter — provides a reliable way to purge Fatal Bonds and interrupt Upheaval’s channel.
Manta Style — creates illusion copies that split the damage of Fatal Bonds and force Warlock to waste spells on multiple targets.
Black King Bar — makes you immune to Shadow Word’s damage/heal component and prevents Upheaval’s slow from affecting you.
Scythe of Vyse — a hard‑lock that stops Warlock from casting his abilities during crucial moments, denying imp spawns.

weaver.name: Weaver
weaver.guideHtml:
Weaver remains a high‑mobility carry with strong escape tools, but his overall win‑rate has slipped to 47.0% on the current 7.41 meta (223 k+ ranked games). He thrives on split‑pushing and pick‑offs, yet struggles against heroes that can lock him down or out‑damage him early.

How to Play Weaver

Laning Phase

  • Shukuchi early levels to dodge harass and secure last hits; the movement‑speed boost also lets you scout enemy jungle for early information.
  • Use The Swarm on enemy creep waves to lower their armor and accelerate lane equilibrium, especially against melee cores that rely on high‑damage right‑clicks.
  • When you spot a risky gank, drop Geminate Attack on the first auto‑attack to double the damage and force the opponent to retreat, buying time for your support’s defensive abilities.
  • Against lane opponents with strong disables (e.g., Shadow Demon, Venomancer), keep a 700‑unit buffer so you can trigger Threads of Fate and tie them to your movement, making it harder for them to land spells.

Mid Game

  • Time Lapse spikes at level 6 and 12; use it to survive burst damage from heroes like Morphling or Sniper, then reposition for a counter‑gank.
  • Prioritize split‑pushing lanes with Shukuchi + The Swarm to force towers down while staying out of enemy vision.
  • Group with a support that provides vision (e.g., Crystal Maiden, Dazzle) and look for 2‑v‑1 picks; your mobility lets you initiate with Shukuchi, burst with Geminate Attack, and escape with Time Lapse.

Late Game

  • Win condition: force the enemy to chase you across the map, using Shukuchi to create chaos and Time Lapse to survive any focused fire.
  • Position near high‑ground or trees to maximize the surprise factor of Shukuchi and to give your team time to react to your Threads of Fate tether.
  • Losing the game usually comes from being caught without Time Lapse cooldown (e.g., after a prolonged team fight) or from heroes that can silence/disarm you (e.g., Shadow Demon, Centaur Warrunner).

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango + Healing Salve — sustain against harass in solo lanes.
  • Iron Branch ×2 — cheap stat boost; can later be used for Magic Wand.
  • Faerie Fire — emergency burst damage to finish low‑HP creeps or deter early ganks.

Core Items

  • Power Treads — flexible stats and attack speed for Geminate Attack.
  • Manta Style — adds extra illusion damage, synergizes with The Swarm armor reduction, and provides a second escape via the active.
  • Butterfly — massive evasion and damage; essential against right‑click heroes like Sniper and Morphling.
  • Satanic — gives you a reliable survivability tool to activate after a Time Lapse‑escape.

Situational Items

  • Black King Bar — when facing heavy magical burst (e.g., Ancient Apparition, Shadow Demon).
  • Eye of Skadi — against heroes with high attack speed or burst (e.g., Morphling, Sniper).
  • Linken’s Sphere — blocks single‑target disables such as Centaur’s Hoof Stomp or Venomancer’s Poison Nova.
  • Mekansm / Guardian Greaves — if your team lacks reliable healing and you need to stay alive in team fights.
  • Abyssal Blade — gives you a stun to lock down elusive heroes like Monkey King or Morphling.

Common Mistakes

  • Wasting Shukuchi on farming – use it for scouting, escaping, or initiating, not just for extra movement speed.
  • Casting Time Lapse too early – you lose the five‑second safety window; hold it for when you’re actually low on HP or about to be focused.
  • Ignoring Threads of Fate – failing to stay within 700 units of an enemy after damaging them forfeits a valuable tether that can limit their escape.
  • Over‑extending without vision – Weaver’s split‑push is powerful, but without wards he becomes an easy target for heroes like Centaur or Shadow Demon.

FAQ

Is Weaver good in the current patch?

Weaver’s win‑rate sits at 47 %, below average, indicating a tougher meta. He still shines in split‑push and pick‑off scenarios, but his effectiveness drops against burst‑damage heroes such as Morphling and Sniper, where his win‑rates are under 35 %.

What lane does Weaver play?

Weaver is typically played in the safe lane as a carry, often paired with a support that can provide early vision and defensive disables (e.g., Crystal Maiden, Dazzle). This lane gives him the farm needed to hit his core items while allowing safe use of Shukuchi to dodge harassment.

Who counters Weaver?

The hardest match‑ups are Morphling (29.4 % win), Sniper (33.3 %), Monkey King (35.3 %), Venomancer (37.0 %), Shadow Demon (38.3 %), and Centaur Warrunner (38.6 %). These heroes either out‑damage him, lock him down, or negate his mobility, making them the primary counters on patch 7.41.
weaver.counterHtml:
Weaver’s strength lies in his insane mobility, burst damage, and the ability to rewind damage with Time Lapse. The most reliable way to shut him down is to force him into a position where he cannot escape or reset, and to punish his low early‑game health pool before his Shukuchi‑enabled hit‑and‑run becomes sustainable.

Why These Heroes Beat Weaver

Morphling

Morphling’s Morph and Waveform let him close the distance on Weaver while instantly adjusting his attribute balance to out‑damage the Swarm and Geminate Attack. A well‑timed Adaptive Strike on a low‑HP Weaver before he can Shukuchi away wipes him before Time Lapse can save him. Tip: Keep Morphling’s Attribute Shift on the high‑damage side and use Waveform to block Weaver’s escape routes.

Sniper

Sniper’s extreme range forces Weaver to rely on Shukuchi just to get into attack range, exposing him to the long‑range Headshot and Assassinate damage that outpaces Weaver’s HP regeneration. The Assassinate stun also prevents Weaver from using Time Lapse to escape after a burst. Tip: Position Sniper on high ground and use Take Aim to increase attack range, making Weaver’s approach even riskier.

Monkey King

Monkey King’s Tree Dance and Boundless Strike give him both vision and a reliable escape that outmatches Weaver’s Shukuchi. The Jungle Smash stun interrupts Weaver’s combo, and Wukong’s Command creates a zone where Weaver’s Swarm is quickly killed, denying his armor‑shredding threat. Tip: Use Tree Dance to keep an eye on Weaver’s movement and punish his re‑engagement attempts with a quick Boundless Strike.

Venomancer

Venomancer’s Poison Nova and Venomous Gale apply massive damage over time that Weaver cannot cleanse, while the slow prevents him from using Shukuchi effectively. The Poison Sting tick damage quickly brings Weaver’s health below the threshold where Time Lapse can rescue him. Tip: Stack multiple poison sources (e.g., Poison Nova + Poison Sting) before Weaver can blink away, forcing a premature death.

Shadow Demon

Shadow Demon’s Disruption instantly removes Weaver from combat, canceling Geminate Attack and Swarm damage, and the subsequent Shadow Poison deals continuous damage that bypasses Weaver’s armor reduction. The Demonic Purge also strips positive buffs, negating any temporary armor or movement speed items Weaver might have. Tip: Time Disruption just after Weaver lands a Shukuchi for a guaranteed stun and follow up with Shadow Poison while he’s trapped.

Drafting Against Weaver

  • Prioritize heroes with strong disables or long‑range burst (e.g., Sniper, Morphling, Shadow Demon).
  • Pick heroes that can apply consistent damage over time and slow (Venomancer, Shadow Demon).
  • Include at least one hero with a reliable escape or vision tool to track Weaver’s Shukuchi (e.g., Monkey King, Earthshaker).
  • Consider banning high‑mobility heroes that could synergize with Weaver’s split‑push (e.g., Anti‑Mage, Puck) to limit his late‑game scaling.

Laning Against Weaver

  • Harass early with ranged attacks and keep the lane wave near your tower to deny safe Shukuchi escapes.
  • Force Weaver to use Shukuchi defensively; each use costs mana and leaves him vulnerable to a follow‑up stun or burst.
  • Trade when his Swarm is on cooldown; his damage output drops dramatically without it.
  • Use vision (wards, true sight) to anticipate his Shukuchi entry point and punish the re‑engagement.

Itemizing Against Weaver

Ghost Scepter — blocks physical damage from Geminate Attack and Swarm, buying time to land disables.
Scythe of Vyse — provides a hard‑lock that Weaver cannot escape with Shukuchi or Time Lapse.
Aghanim’s Shard (Monkey King) — grants Tree Dance vision and a stun that interrupts his mobility.
Eul’s Scepter of Divinity — lifts Weaver out of combat, nullifying his Shukuchi and resetting his combo cooldowns.

windranger.name: Windranger
windranger.guideHtml:
Windranger remains a versatile pick in patch 7.41, swinging between a high‑damage core and a slippery support. With a 48.2 % win rate across over half‑a‑million ranked games, she sits near the middle of the hero popularity curve but still offers strong pick‑off potential when played correctly.

How to Play Windranger

Laning Phase

  • Use Shackleshot early to punish aggressive melee heroes; the stun is longer when you can chain to a tree or ally creep.
  • Harass with Powershot—charge just enough to land a slow on the enemy while conserving mana for the next wave.
  • Pair Windrun with a defensive tower block to dodge incoming harass from heroes like Bane or Dazzle, whose win rates against her are above 40 %.
  • If you’re a support, stack Gale Force on the creep wave to push the lane and force the enemy off‑lane, especially effective against push‑heavy heroes like Treant Protector.
  • Keep an eye on Tailwind stacks; a quick burst of movement speed can save you from ganks or let you close the distance for a Shackleshot combo.

Mid Game

  • Power Spike: 20 / 20 / 20 / 20 / 20 / 20 (level 6) – unlocks Windrun and Gale Force; start rotating for pick‑offs.
  • Prioritize vision around Roshan and high‑ground jungle; a well‑timed Shackleshot into a tree can secure a solo kill on squishy targets like Morphling or Oracle (both > 60 % win vs. Windranger).
  • Use Focus Fire on towers or high‑HP heroes when you have a reliable Windrun escape; the damage reduction is offset by item procs (e.g., Maelstrom).
  • Avoid extended team fights against Enigma, Treant Protector, or Naga Siren—your win rates are under 37 % in those matchups; instead look for isolated pick‑offs.

Late Game

  • Win condition: pick off key carries with Shackleshot + Windrun followed by a Powershot burst, then force the enemy to waste Black King Bar or Aghanim’s Scepter.
  • Position near trees or cliffs to guarantee a secondary target for Shackleshot; without it the stun drops to 0.6 s and you lose crowd‑control value.
  • Losing the game usually stems from over‑committing without Windrun cooldown or getting caught by AoE ultimates (e.g., Enigma’s Black Hole, Treant’s Overgrowth).

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango — sustain in lane, especially against harass from Bane or Dazzle.
  • Healing Salve — quick health recovery after early ganks.
  • Iron Branch ×2 — cheap stats and can later be used for a Magic Wand.
  • Slippers of Agility — early damage boost for Powershot and Focus Fire.

Core Items

  • Power Treads — attack speed for Focus Fire and movement speed for better positioning.
  • Maelstrom — amplifies the reduced‑damage Focus Fire with chain lightning, essential for mid‑game tower pressure.
  • Dragon Lance — adds range and damage, making Shackleshot and Powershot safer from enemy counter‑initiations.
  • Manta Style — provides a second Windrun charge and removes silences from Bane or Dazzle.

Situational Items

  • Eul’s Scepter — extra disable and a second escape tool against heroes like Enigma.
  • Black King Bar — mandatory when facing heavy magical burst (e.g., Enigma, Treant).
  • Satanic — survivability in prolonged fights, especially against tankier foes like Alchemist.
  • Gleipnir — adds a strong AoE slow to complement Shackleshot in team fights.
  • Aghanim’s Scepter — upgrades Shackleshot to affect multiple units, turning you into a true team‑fight controller against heroes like Phantom Lancer.

Common Mistakes

  • Over‑charging Powershot – wasting mana and leaving yourself vulnerable; a half‑second charge is usually enough for a kill.
  • Using Shackleshot without a secondary target – the stun drops to 0.6 s, making it ineffective.
  • Neglecting Windrun cooldown – many low‑MMR players spam it early and get caught without it later.
  • Building pure damage items – ignoring survivability leads to easy deaths against high‑control matchups (Treant, Enigma).

FAQ

Is Windranger good in the current patch?

Yes. Her 48.2 % win rate shows she’s viable, especially as a pick‑off hero. She excels against squishy carries like Oracle and Morphling (≈ 62 % win) but struggles versus heavy‑control heroes such as Treant Protector and Enigma.

What lane does Windranger play?

Windranger can be played both safely in the safe lane (as a support) or aggressively in the off‑lane (as a core). The lane choice depends on your team’s draft: safe‑lane support for vision and pick‑offs, off‑lane core for early tower pressure.

Who counters Windranger?

Heroes with strong area control and low % win rates against her are the biggest threats: Treant Protector (30.8 % win), Naga Siren (34.0 %), Enigma (36.9 %), Bane (37.5 %), Dazzle (40.6 %), and Alchemist (41.5 %). Their abilities can neutralize her mobility and prevent effective Shackleshot combos.
windranger.counterHtml:

Why These Heroes Beat Windranger

Treant Protector

Treant’s Nature’s Guise grants true‑sight and a brief invisibility window, letting him dodge Shackleshot and set up surprise Leech Seed on a fleeing Windranger. His Overgrowth creates a massive, hard‑to‑escape stun that negates Windrun’s evasion and forces a vulnerable channel. Tip: keep a tree or two between you and Treant’s Overgrowth radius to avoid being caught while you’re channeling Powershot.

Naga Siren

Naga’s Mirror Image provides instant damage‑block and confusion, making it hard for Windranger to land a clean Shackleshot. When she activates Riptide, the slow and damage stack quickly overwhelm Windrun’s evasion, and Ensnare can root Windranger mid‑channel. Tip: force Naga to use Mirror Image early by trading aggressively, then follow up with a Powershot while she’s on cooldown.

Enigma

Enigma’s Midnight Pulse deals pure damage in a large area, punishing Windranger’s tendency to stay in lane and farm with Powershot. Black Hole nullifies Windrun’s evasion and forces a guaranteed Shackleshot‑free stun, wiping out her mobility. Tip: buy early Mekansm or Pipe to mitigate Black Hole’s damage and give your team a chance to disengage.

Bane

Bane’s Nightmare and Enfeeble heavily reduce Windranger’s attack damage and interrupt her channeling of Powershot and Focus Fire. His ultimate Fiend’s Grip applies a long‑duration disable that ignores Windrun’s evasion, leaving Windranger helpless. Tip: keep a Sentry Ward near your lane to spot Bane’s positioning and punish him when he overextends with Nightmare.

Dazzle

Dazzle’s Shallow Grave can block the lethal burst from a fully‑charged Powershot, forcing Windranger to waste her channel. His Shadow Wave provides constant healing, outlasting the damage from Shackleshot and reducing the incentive for aggressive trades. Tip: time your own Gale Force or Powershot just after Dazzle casts Shadow Wave to catch him while his shield is on cooldown.

Drafting Against Windranger

  • Prioritize heroes with hard disables (stuns/root) that can interrupt Shackleshot or channeling (e.g., Enigma, Bane).
  • Choose high‑burst magic damage heroes to outrange her 48 % win rate (e.g., Lina, Lion).
  • Pick mobile heroes with strong lane sustain to survive her early harass (e.g., Juggernaut, Lifestealer).
  • Consider anti‑evasion items or abilities (e.g., True Strike, Diffusal Blade) to blunt Windrun.

Laning Against Windranger

  • Trade when Windranger is channeling Powershot or Focus Fire; the cast time leaves her vulnerable.
  • Harass aggressively before she gets Windrun level 2, as her evasion is weakest early.
  • Force her to use Shackleshot on a tree rather than a hero by positioning near neutral creeps or trees.
  • Punish her after a missed Shackleshot—she’s often out of position and can be ganked.

Itemizing Against Windranger

Mekansm — provides burst heal and armor to survive her Powershot burst and Overgrowth from Enigma.
Pipe of Insight — blocks magical damage from her combined Powershot + Shackleshot burst and from heroes that synergize with her.
Diffusal Blade — burns mana, shortening the window for Shackleshot and Windrun, and adds a purge against slows.
Eul’s Scepter — cyclone can interrupt her channel and remove her evasion temporarily, setting up a counter‑engage.

The key to shutting her down is to limit her spacing, punish her channel times, and apply sustained pressure that outpaces her escape tools.

faq.a: Yes. Her 48.2 % win rate shows she’s viable, especially as a pick‑off hero. She excels against squishy carries like Oracle and Morphling (≈ 62 % win) but struggles versus heavy‑control heroes such as Treant Protector and Enigma.

Windranger can be played both safely in the safe lane (as a support) or aggressively in the off‑lane (as a core). The lane choice depends on your team’s draft: safe‑lane support for vision and pick‑offs, off‑lane core for early tower pressure.

Heroes with strong area control and low % win rates against her are the biggest threats: Treant Protector (30.8 % win), Naga Siren (34.0 %), Enigma (36.9 %), Bane (37.5 %), Dazzle (40.6 %), and Alchemist (41.5 %). Their abilities can neutralize her mobility and prevent effective Shackleshot combos.

winter-wyvern.name: Winter Wyvern
winter-wyvern.guideHtml:
Winter Wyvern is a utility‑heavy support whose kit revolves around strong single‑target disables, massive healing, and zone control. In the current 7.41 meta she sits at a 49.1% win rate over 161 k recent ranked games, making her a solid but not dominant pick. Her strength lies in protecting carries and punishing aggressive melee heroes, while she struggles against heroes that can out‑burst or bypass her disables.

How to Play Winter Wyvern

Laning Phase

  • Arctic Burn early levels gives you free movement and a short‑range attack speed boost; use it to harass and secure last hits when the lane is safe.
  • Splinter Blast is a cheap poke tool—aim the splash toward enemy supports or off‑lane heroes to chip health and force them to retreat.
  • Cold Embrace on yourself or your core when the lane is contested can block physical damage from aggressive off‑laners like Axe or Ember Spirit.
  • Prioritize Winter’s Curse on the enemy carry when they dive; the forced attack on the frozen ally can turn a 2‑vs‑1 into a kill.
  • Against hard‑disabling lane partners (e.g., Ogre Magi, Windranger) keep your Cold Embrace cooldown ready and stay near your tower to avoid being caught by their burst.

Mid Game

  • Power spike at level 6: Winter’s Curse now has a longer stun and the aura damage increases, making you a potent initiator in skirmishes.
  • Roam with Arctic Burn to create vision and set up ganks; the movement speed boost lets you cross the river quickly.
  • Pair Cold Embrace with a strong frontline (e.g., Slardar) to create an “unkillable” pocket for your core during team fights.
  • Use Splinter Blast in clustered fights; the 500 radius splash can punish heroes that group tightly like Snapfire or Puck.

Late Game

  • Win condition: protect your hyper‑carry with Cold Embrace while forcing enemies into your Winter’s Curse zone; the forced attacks often disrupt enemy positioning and allow your team to focus priority targets.
  • Positioning: stay just behind your front line; your Arctic Burn gives you the freedom to reposition without being caught on cooldown.
  • Losing the game often comes from over‑extending without a Cold Embrace ready, allowing burst heroes (Axe, Ember Spirit) to eliminate you and open the fight.

Item Build

Starting Items

  • Tango — sustain for the early lane.
  • Healing Salve — quick health recovery after early harass.
  • Observer Ward — vision to avoid ganks and set up early Winter’s Curse plays.
  • Clarity ×2 — mana for early Splinter Blast spam.

Core Items

  • Tranquil Boots — movement speed for roaming with Arctic Burn and passive HP regen.
  • Glimmer Cape — additional magic shield for yourself or a carry when you need to survive burst.
  • Mekansm → Guardian Greaves — burst heal and armor; synergizes with Cold Embrace’s healing.
  • Aghanim’s Shard — upgrades Splinter Blast to apply a brief slow, increasing its utility in team fights.

Situational Items

  • Lotus Orb — reflects single‑target disables that can otherwise lock you down (e.g., from Ogre Magi).
  • Force Staff — extra mobility to escape when your Arctic Burn is on cooldown.
  • Ghost Scepter — against right‑click heavy heroes like Axe or Ember Spirit when you need to avoid physical damage.
  • Aeon Disk — prevents instant death from burst combos, buying time to cast Cold Embrace.
  • Shiva’s Guard — adds armor and an AoE slow, amplifying the impact of Winter’s Curse in clustered fights.

Common Mistakes

  • Casting Cold Embrace on the wrong target – using it on an enemy or a low‑HP ally instead of your core wastes the biggest defensive tool.
  • Over‑relying on Splinter Blast damage – the ability’s primary target takes no damage; many players forget the splash radius and miss the true damage potential.
  • Holding Winter’s Curse for a perfect moment – waiting too long often lets the enemy escape; use it proactively to force a frozen ally into a vulnerable position.
  • Neglecting vision – without wards, you cannot safely roam with Arctic Burn, and enemies can pick off your support before you can react.

FAQ

Is Winter Wyvern good in the current patch?

Yes. With a 49.1% win rate across 161 k recent ranked matches, Winter Wyvern is a viable support. Her strong defensive tools and team‑fight control keep her relevant, especially against melee front‑liners.

What lane does Winter Wyvern play?

Winter Wyvern is typically played as a hard support in the safe lane (radiant bottom or dire top). She can also be flexed to off‑lane support when a teammate can handle the primary farm.

Who counters Winter Wyvern?

Heroes that can burst her before she lands Cold Embrace or that have strong magical damage are toughest: Ogre Magi (38.7% win rate vs. her), Windranger (39.7%), Snapfire (39.8%), Axe (40.0%), Ember Spirit (40.7%), and Lich (42.6%). Building early Lotus Orb or Ghost Scepter can mitigate their impact.
winter-wyvern.counterHtml:
Winter Wyvern’s strength lies in her burst heal + damage combo and the game‑changing crowd‑control of Winter’s Curse, which can lock down a team and turn an ally into a damage sponge. To shut her down you must deny her the chance to land a successful Curse on a high‑damage target and force her into early fights where her low base damage and lack of escape leave her vulnerable.

Why These Heroes Beat Winter Wyvern

Ogre Magi

Ogre’s Fireblast provides a reliable stun that can interrupt Winter’s Arctic Burn and prevent her from positioning for a Curse. His Multicast on Ignite or Bloodlust also adds burst damage that overwhelms Winter’s modest attack damage.
Tip: Use Fireblast on Winter Wyvern as soon as she initiates; the stun also blocks her Cold Embrace from saving an ally.

Windranger

Windranger’s Shackles can lock Winter Wyvern in place before she can activate Winter’s Curse, and her Windrun grants magic immunity that blocks the Curse’s debuff. Her high‑damage Focus Fire exploits Winter’s low health pool.
Tip: Aim Shackles at Winter while she’s mid‑air on Arctic Burn; the stun will cancel the flight and leave her exposed.

Snapfire

Snapfire’s Cookie provides a strong heal shield that counters Winter’s Cold Embrace block, while Firesnap Cookie can burst‑damage Winter before she can cast Curse. Her Scatterblast offers a reliable stun that interrupts Winter’s combo.
Tip: Drop a Cookie on the ally you intend to protect; the heal shield will negate the healing Winter tries to give and force her to waste Cold Embrace.

Axe

Axe’s Berserker’s Call forces Winter Wyvern to attack him, breaking the synergy of Winter’s Curse that makes enemies attack the frozen ally. His Counter Helix punishes any melee attacks Winter makes while she’s trying to chase.
Tip: Initiate with Call as soon as Winter lands her Arctic Burn; the forced melee attack nullifies her ranged advantage and can quickly kill her.

Ember Spirit

Ember’s Sleight of Fist provides burst magical damage that bypasses Winter’s physical‑damage block from Cold Embrace, and his Flame Guard grants magic immunity that blocks the Curse’s debuff. Ember’s high mobility lets him dodge Winter’s Arctic Burn.
Tip: Activate Flame Guard before Winter casts Winter’s Curse; the magic immunity prevents the Curse from applying and lets you close the distance for a kill.

Drafting Against Winter Wyvern

  • Prioritize hard‑disable heroes (stuns, silences) that can interrupt Arctic Burn and Winter’s Curse.
  • Pick magic‑immune or magic‑resistant heroes to nullify the Curse’s damage amplification.
  • Choose early‑game burst damage heroes to exploit her low base damage before she can level her heal.
  • Consider bans that remove strong anti‑heal or anti‑crowd‑control options (e.g., Silencer, Oracle).

Laning Against Winter Wyvern

  • Harass her early; she has low damage and relies on getting a level 2 Cold Embrace to be safe.
  • Trade when she is out of Arctic Burn cooldown—she cannot reposition or escape.
  • Punish any attempt to Cold Embrace an ally by focusing the protected hero; the shield blocks physical damage but not your magical burst.
  • Keep lane creeps stacked to force her to use Splinter Blast on minions, wasting its AoE potential.

Itemizing Against Winter Wyvern

Black King Bar — grants magic immunity, blocking Winter’s Curse and the damage amplification it provides.
Heaven’s Halberd — disarms Winter Wyvern, preventing her from delivering the attacks that trigger Winter’s Curse.
Mekansm / Guardian Greaves — provides a strong heal shield that counters the healing from Cold Embrace and can save allies from being frozen.
Diffusal Blade — burns mana, shortening the window for her to cast Arctic Burn and Winter’s Curse.
